hints: Focus on what each statement is really testing, oxidising strength, volatility trend, simple stoichiometry, and reducing power of halides.
Recall that oxidising power decreases down Group 17 but never reaches zero, and that bigger molecules have stronger London forces so are less volatile.
Write the equation for hydrogen with chlorine and check the mole ratio, then remember how far bromide versus iodide can reduce concentrated sulfuric acid.
walkthrough:
**Check oxidising ability down the group**

All halogens can gain an electron to form halide ions, so all can act as oxidising agents. The power just gets weaker down the group: $\text{Cl}_2 > \text{Br}_2 > \text{I}_2$.

Example with iodine:
$$\text{I}_2 + 2\text{S}_2\text{O}_3^{2-} \rightarrow 2\text{I}^- + \text{S}_4\text{O}_6^{2-}$$

**Check volatility trend**

Volatility means how easily a liquid or solid turns to vapour. From chlorine to iodine, molecular size and electrons increase.

This gives stronger London forces, higher boiling points, and lower volatility. So $\text{Cl}_2$ (gas) is most volatile, $\text{I}_2$ (solid) is least volatile.

**Check hydrogen plus chlorine reaction**

Hydrogen burns explosively in chlorine in a simple 1:1 combination reaction.

$$\text{H}_2 + \text{Cl}_2 \rightarrow 2\text{HCl}$$
An equimolar mixture matches this ratio exactly, so only hydrogen chloride is formed.

**Check concentrated sulfuric acid with sodium bromide**

Concentrated $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ first makes $\text{HBr}$, then $\text{HBr}$ reduces the acid to $\text{SO}_2$ and is itself oxidised to $\text{Br}_2$.

$$2\text{HBr} + \text{H}_2\text{SO}_4 \rightarrow \text{Br}_2 + \text{SO}_2 + 2\text{H}_2\text{O}$$
Bromide is not strong enough to reduce sulfur all the way to $\text{H}_2\text{S}$. That only happens with iodide.

options.A: Incorrect. Iodine is the weakest oxidising agent of chlorine, bromine and iodine, but it still oxidises. For example, it oxidises thiosulfate to tetrathionate and is reduced to iodide. Weaker does not mean unable.
options.B: Incorrect. This reverses the trend. Larger molecules from chlorine to iodine have more electrons and stronger London forces, so boiling point increases and volatility decreases. Iodine is a solid, chlorine is a gas.
options.C: Correct. The reaction is H2 + Cl2 -> 2HCl. An equimolar (1:1) mixture is exactly the stoichiometric ratio, so both reactants are fully used up to give hydrogen chloride as the single product.
options.D: Incorrect. With NaBr, concentrated sulfuric acid gives HBr, then Br2 and SO2. Hydrogen sulfide, where sulfur is reduced from +6 to -2, is only formed with NaI because iodide is a much stronger reducing agent than bromide.
